description:
This is the official participating delegation from BMTL school 🏫. All participating school members shall join this group only. The topic chosen is beginner friendly and curated for best possible outcome. Moreover the Challenge chosen is Abandoned but not forgotten (story telling module)🔭🌓.

Since It is a simple challenge we are looking for people who can tell stories exceptionally and can visually 👀 show it instead of making power point presentations.
summary:
We made a website covering different machines that humans have left behind on the Moon and Mars. It's mainly aimed at teenagers, but we also wanted younger children to understand and connect with the machines through their stories.
We created a fictional scenario where these machines had feelings and could tell us about their experiences, what they did and what they achieved during their missions. At the end, we included the lessons we could learn from them and the legacy they left behind.
One thing we really wanted to highlight was that even if these machines had feelings, they still achieved something, no matter how small. Every little contribution mattered towards human advancement, and that's the main message we wanted people to take away from our project.
details:
"Abandoned, but not forgotten" is a story-led website which takes school-age space fans through the NASA spacecraft that are currently left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Rather than a very dry history, the spacecraft tell their own stories. Each one (Eagle, Intrepid, Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity) tells their own tale in the first person, following the same structure: a hook, where they came from, their mission, what they discovered, where they are now and why they matter.

The home page is a star map with thirteen retired spacecraft glowing as stars above a view of the Earth. Each one has a card which pops up with its launch date, its purpose, its end date and where it is now, plus a link to its NASA record. There are nine story pages covering the Moon (in four parts) and Mars (in five parts). Each page has a facts grid and a panel of data taken from the NASA records. Key lines are highlighted and at the end of each page the highlighted letters fall apart and float to form a single sentence which summarises the page.

We built it for young readers. It has book style text, a read aloud button, larger/smaller text buttons and a tap for meaning word help. It works on phones and is compatible with reduced motion settings.

Facts are drawn from NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive and from the NASA Science mission pages (all sources are listed on the Sources page). The machines’ thoughts are entirely fictional and the site makes that very clear. AI was used and is fully disclosed on the Sources page: Claude was used to write the code and the illustrations and to check the facts, and the team wrote the stories and selected the content. It was all built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript and is hosted on GitHub.
